items.stemHtml:
A 46-year-old woman has 2 months of fatigue, nausea and loss of appetite. She had a severe sudden headache 4 months ago that resolved without evaluation. She takes no medications. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure 104/66 mmHg without orthostatic change; she is clinically euvolemic. Skin colour is normal. Laboratory studies:

TestResult
Serum sodium125 mEq/L
Serum potassium4.1 mEq/L
Glucose74 mg/dL
Serum osmolality262 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality460 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium52 mEq/L
TSH1.2 µU/mL
Free thyroxine (T4)0.6 ng/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine and a high urine sodium looks like SIADH, but SIADH can be diagnosed only after adrenal and thyroid insufficiency are excluded. A low free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH means central hypothyroidism, and the earlier thunderclap headache suggests pituitary apoplexy, so she may also have secondary adrenal insufficiency. Cortisol deficiency raises ADH and causes this exact picture; potassium stays normal because aldosterone is preserved. Measure morning cortisol (and treat with hydrocortisone if she is unwell or it is low) before levothyroxine, which could otherwise precipitate adrenal crisis.

Takeaway: never label euvolemic hyponatremia as SIADH until cortisol (and thyroid) deficiency is excluded; in central hypothyroidism, check and replace cortisol before thyroxine.

whyNot.A: Fluid restriction treats SIADH, but secondary adrenal insufficiency has not been excluded and would be missed.
whyNot.C: Starting thyroxine before assessing cortisol can unmask adrenal crisis by speeding cortisol metabolism.
whyNot.D: Tolvaptan is not used before a cause is found and could correct sodium too fast.
whyNot.E: Salt tablets treat SIADH-type hyponatremia and would leave the hormonal cause undiagnosed.

items.objective: Exclude secondary adrenal insufficiency before diagnosing SIADH, especially with central hypothyroidism.
